opus-5.5.text:
Dense architectures like Llama's are very clean and stable, and that's a real strength. But when you keep scaling them, the core limitation is cost: every parameter is activated for every token. If you want more knowledge and capability, you add parameters, and training and inference compute grow right along with them. At some point the cost curve gets very steep.

That's what pushed many of us toward sparse architectures like Mixture-of-Experts. With MoE you can greatly increase total parameters, so the model's capacity and knowledge grow, while each token only activates a small fraction of them. You decouple "how much the model knows" from "how much compute each token costs." For a team without unlimited GPUs, that matters a lot.

The second limitation is inference, especially memory. With standard attention, the KV cache grows with sequence length and batch size, and for long contexts it becomes the bottleneck. Serving gets expensive, throughput drops, and long-context use gets hard to deploy. So beyond the feed-forward layers, we also had to rethink attention, for example compressing the KV cache so the model can be served much more efficiently.

To me, scaling isn't just about making models bigger. It's about making the architecture efficient enough that you can afford to scale. Dense models aren't wrong, but if you only follow that path, you're competing purely on compute. Architecture innovation is how you get more capability per unit of compute, and I think that's where much of the real progress has come from.

r001.rationale: It describes dense-model scaling costs becoming steep, but does not identify scaling to several hundred billion parameters as the practical limit.

r002.rationale: “Dense models aren’t wrong” does not convey that Llama’s large-model outcomes fail to establish an inherent architectural problem.

r003.rationale: It says dense scaling costs pushed researchers toward sparse architectures such as Mixture-of-Experts.

fable-5.1.text:
Dense architectures like Llama are very clean and very well understood, which is exactly why they scale predictably. But the limitation is simple: every token activates every parameter. If you want the model to know more, you make it bigger, and then every forward pass pays the full cost of that size, both in training compute and in inference.

So you end up on a curve where capacity and cost are locked together. At 70B or 400B dense, each token is doing the same amount of work whether the input is trivial or genuinely hard. That is wasteful. A lot of what a large model stores is specialized knowledge that only matters for a small slice of inputs, yet you compute through all of it every time.

This is why I think sparsity, mixture-of-experts in particular, is the more natural direction. You can keep growing total parameters, which is what gives you knowledge and capability, while keeping the activated parameters per token roughly fixed. That decouples the two axes. Our experience with DeepSeek-V2 and V3 was that you could get strong quality with a fraction of the activated compute, and that gap only widens as you push total parameters up.

The honest caveat is that MoE is harder to train well. Load balancing, expert routing, communication overhead across devices, these are real engineering problems, and a dense model avoids all of them. So Llama's choice is defensible as a reliable baseline. But if the question is where the ceiling is, I think dense hits a cost wall long before it hits a capability wall, and sparse architectures move that wall.

r001.rationale: It says that at 400B parameters, every token incurs the full compute cost and describes dense scaling as hitting a cost wall.

r002.rationale: It calls Llama’s dense approach a defensible baseline, but does not state that results from its large models fail to establish an inherent architectural problem.

r003.rationale: It presents mixture-of-experts as a response to dense models’ cost, allowing total parameters to grow while keeping activated parameters per token roughly fixed.

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is that, in a dense architecture, every token activates all the parameters. So as you make the model larger, the computation required for both training and inference grows with it. You can add capacity, but you also make that capacity more expensive to use.

A mixture-of-experts architecture gives you another way to scale: you increase the total number of parameters while activating only a subset for each token. That introduces challenges in routing, load balancing, and communication, but it lets you grow model capacity without increasing computation as much as a dense model would.

r001.rationale: It says dense-model computation grows with size and becomes more expensive, but does not identify prohibitive cost as a practical limit at several hundred billion parameters.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether Llama’s large dense-model outcomes establish an inherent architectural problem.

r003.rationale: It presents mixture-of-experts as another way to scale capacity while limiting per-token computation, directly connecting it to dense models’ rising computational expense.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main limitation is that, in a dense architecture, every token activates all the parameters. So as you scale the model, you also increase the computation required for every token, both during training and inference. You can add more capacity, but it becomes increasingly expensive to use that capacity.

A mixture-of-experts architecture offers a different tradeoff: you can increase the total number of parameters while activating only a subset for each token. That doesn’t make scaling free—you still have challenges with routing, load balancing, and communication—but it gives you more flexibility to grow capacity without increasing computation at the same rate.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether results from Llama’s large dense models establish an inherent architectural problem.
